evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG.

rules.text: No single ideal macronutrient split. The ADA endorses several eating patterns with evidence: Mediterranean-style, low-carbohydrate, plant-based, and DASH. The 2026 Standards added patient-facing resources for Mediterranean-style and low-carb patterns, especially for prevention.
Emphasize non-starchy vegetables and prefer whole foods over highly processed ones.
Minimize added sugars and refined grains.
Carbohydrate quality and quantity both matter. Monitoring carbohydrate intake is the primary strategy for glycemic control. The Diabetes Plate method is the ADA's default teaching tool.

If you have overweight or obesity, a 5 to 7 percent weight loss improves glycemia and cardiometabolic risk; over 10 percent can produce remission. Calorie restriction is appropriate here, but the ADA frames it as individualized, not universal. Whether calories are foregrounded follows your priority goals.
Avoid sugar-sweetened beverages.
Non-nutritive sweeteners are an acceptable short-term replacement, with the goal of reducing overall sweet intake.
Sodium under 2,300 mg/day, same as the general population.
rules.why: Sodium under 2,300 mg a day, the same as the general population.

rules.text: Alcohol: moderate at most. If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, be aware of hypoglycemia risk with alcohol.
Fiber at least the general population target (14 g per 1,000 kcal). Higher intake from whole grains, legumes, and vegetables improves glycemia.
rules.why: Whole grains (oats, brown rice, barley, whole-wheat bread), legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas), and vegetables raise fiber, and higher fiber from these foods improves glycemia.

rules.text: If you take insulin or a GLP-1 medication, your plan needs to be set with your clinician. The app supports that plan; it does not set targets.

conflicts.text: Strong interaction with the lipid rules; DASH and Mediterranean already satisfy both.
Strong interaction with the hypertension rules; DASH and Mediterranean already satisfy both.
Long-term low-histamine restriction conflicts with diabetes eating patterns; the time limit is the safeguard.
Fully compatible with diabetes rules. This condition rarely travels alone.
Low-carb is one ADA-endorsed pattern for T2D. Insulin, sulfonylurea, and SGLT2 use require the medication screen and clinician input before starting.
Diabetes in pregnancy (ADA Section 15) and GDM carbohydrate targets are clinician-set.
Conflicts with diabetes fiber advice; texture wins, fiber from soluble, cooked, or blended sources. Gastroparesis is common in long-standing diabetes (glucose control affects emptying).

medication_questions.text: Do you take insulin or a sulfonylurea?
Do you take an SGLT2 inhibitor?

education.plain: There is no single right diet for type 2 diabetes. Mediterranean-style, low-carb, plant-based, and DASH patterns all have evidence, and the one you can keep is the one that works. Eat plenty of non-starchy vegetables, cut added sugar and refined grains, skip sugary drinks, and keep an eye on how much carbohydrate you eat. If you carry extra weight, losing 5 to 7 percent helps; if you use insulin or a GLP-1 medication, your clinician sets the plan and this app works around it.
evidence: The ADA endorses several eating patterns with evidence: Mediterranean-style, low-carbohydrate, plant-based, and DASH.
Monitoring carbohydrate intake is the primary strategy for glycemic control; the Diabetes Plate method remains the ADA's default teaching tool.
5 to 7 percent weight loss improves glycemia and cardiometabolic risk in people with overweight or obesity; over 10 percent can produce remission.
Fiber at or above 14 g per 1,000 kcal, and higher intake from whole grains, legumes, and vegetables, improves glycemia.
The Diabetes Prevention Program (NEJM 2002) and its 10 and 15 year follow-ups support lifestyle change for prediabetes.
contested: Very low carbohydrate diets have good short-term glycemic data but weaker long-term adherence data. Low-carb is one valid option, not the answer.
Meal timing and intermittent fasting: emerging, not guideline-level. Some evidence; an individual decision with clinician input.
Calorie counting: the evidence supports weight loss as a goal for many but not all people with T2D. Your priority goals drive whether calories are foregrounded.

A newer ADA nutrition consensus report was said to be expected in 2026; as of September 30, 2026 none has been published, and the 2026 Standards of Care still point to the 2019 report (VERIFY: check again for a new report).
do_not_claim: Do not present low-carb as the answer; it is one valid option.
Do not set carbohydrate or insulin-related targets for people on insulin or GLP-1 medications; the clinician sets the plan.
Do not treat calorie restriction as universal for T2D.
Do not present intermittent fasting as guideline-level advice.

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG.

rules.text: Follow the DASH eating pattern (Class 1, Level A): vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, legumes, nuts.
DASH limits saturated fat, red meat, sweets, and sugar-sweetened beverages.
Limited saturated fat as part of the DASH pattern (no separate number in the hypertension guideline; the heart-healthy module carries the percent-of-calories limit).
Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day, moving toward an ideal under 1,500 mg (Class 1, Level A). Contraindicated in severe symptomatic orthostatic hypotension.
rules.why: Sodium raises blood pressure in most people, potassium from food lowers it, and the overall eating pattern matters more than any single food.

rules.text: Potassium 3,500 to 5,000 mg/day, preferably from food (Class 1, Level A). Exception: chronic kidney disease or drugs that reduce potassium excretion (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, potassium-sparing diuretics), where serum potassium must be monitored.
rules.why: Sodium raises blood pressure in most people, potassium from food lowers it, and the overall eating pattern matters more than any single food.

rules.text: Potassium-based salt substitutes can be useful, with the same exceptions as the potassium target (CKD or potassium-retaining drugs).
Alcohol: reduce or eliminate.
If overweight, at least 5 percent weight loss.

conflicts.text: The hypertension potassium target (3,500 to 5,000 mg) is a hard conflict with CKD. CKD wins; the potassium target and the salt-substitute note are suppressed and the app says why.
Potassium in dialysis is individualized by serum level; the hypertension potassium target is suppressed, as for non-dialysis CKD.
Fully compatible; the Mediterranean pattern satisfies both.
Fully compatible; DASH and Mediterranean satisfy both.
Fully compatible with hypertension rules.
Same sodium ceiling and DASH pattern; heart failure does not push the 1,500 mg ideal.

medication_questions.text: Do you take an ACE inhibitor, ARB, spironolactone, or a potassium-sparing diuretic?

education.plain: The DASH eating pattern is the strongest-evidence diet for blood pressure: vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, legumes, and nuts, with less red meat, sweets, and sugary drinks. Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day and work toward 1,500. Get 3,500 to 5,000 mg of potassium a day from food unless you have kidney disease or take a medication that holds on to potassium. Cut back on alcohol, and if you carry extra weight, losing 5 percent helps.
evidence: DASH eating pattern: Class 1, Level A recommendation in the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline; the DASH trial (NEJM 1997) and DASH-Sodium (NEJM 2001) are the foundational RCTs.
Sodium under 2,300 mg/day, ideally under 1,500 mg/day: Class 1, Level A.
Potassium 3,500 to 5,000 mg/day, preferably from food: Class 1, Level A, with exceptions for CKD and potassium-retaining drugs.
Potassium-enriched salt substitutes reduced stroke in the Salt Substitute and Stroke Study (SSaSS, NEJM 2021).
contested: Population-level sodium targets are debated in the academic literature (some cohort data suggest a J-shaped curve with optimal intake around 3 to 5 g/day). For people who already have hypertension, the guideline position is clear and the app follows it. The debate belongs here in education, not in the rules engine.
do_not_claim: The app must not silently pick a side between hypertension and POTS sodium; it displays the conflict and refuses to generate a sodium target.
The app must not apply the potassium target to someone with CKD or on potassium-retaining drugs without the medication question and suppression.
Do not apply the sodium ideal to someone with severe symptomatic orthostatic hypotension.
Do not claim the plan will lower your blood pressure; the app supports eating in a way that supports healthy blood pressure.

modules.name: Heart-healthy / LDL-lowering
merges: Part B, 14: Low cholesterol / heart-healthy. Same rules, same rating. One heart-healthy module with two entry points (condition: high cholesterol; pattern: heart-healthy).

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG.

rules.text: Replace saturated fat with unsaturated fat (polyunsaturated and monounsaturated). This is the single highest-evidence lever for LDL.
Saturated fat under 10 percent of calories for the general population; under 6 percent is the AHA target for people who need to lower LDL.
rules.why: The single biggest thing you can do for LDL cholesterol is swap saturated fat (butter, fatty meat, full-fat dairy, coconut oil) for unsaturated fat (olive oil, canola oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, fish).

rules.text: Eliminate industrial trans fat.
rules.why: Cut out industrial trans fat completely.

rules.text: Dietary cholesterol has no specific numeric limit in US guidance, but the AHA advisory still recommends a pattern low in cholesterol-rich foods because they travel with saturated fat. Eggs in moderation are acceptable for most people.
Soluble fiber (oats, barley, legumes, psyllium) 5 to 10 g/day lowers LDL modestly.
rules.why: Add soluble fiber: oats, barley, beans, lentils, psyllium. 5 to 10 g a day lowers LDL modestly.

rules.text: Plant sterols/stanols, 2 g/day, lower LDL about 8 to 10 percent. Legitimate, but food-based sources are limited; this borders on supplement territory, so it is presented as an option with the evidence, not a push.
Mediterranean or DASH pattern overall.
Limit added sugar and refined carbohydrate for triglycerides.
Alcohol: limit, especially for high triglycerides.

conflicts.text: Fully compatible; the Mediterranean pattern satisfies all three of diabetes, hypertension, and lipid rules.
Fully compatible; the Mediterranean pattern satisfies all three.
Heart-healthy foods (nuts, fish, tomatoes, citrus, olive oil, legumes) overlap with low-histamine exclusions. Resolved by the elimination time limit plus explicit user acknowledgment (Part D, 4).
Gastroparesis texture rules win over heart-healthy nut and whole-grain advice; meet fiber goals through soluble, cooked, or blended sources where possible.
High-oxalate foods (nuts, spinach, beets) overlap the heart-healthy list; reconcile by pairing with calcium in the same meal rather than eliminating.
Fully compatible with lipid rules.
A low-carb diet built on processed meat and butter is not heart-healthy; the saturated fat limit still applies.

education.plain: The biggest thing you can do for LDL is swap saturated fat (butter, fatty meat, full-fat dairy, coconut oil) for unsaturated fat (olive oil, nuts, seeds, fish). Keep saturated fat under 10 percent of calories, or under 6 percent if you need to lower LDL, and cut out industrial trans fat. Oats, barley, beans, and psyllium add soluble fiber that lowers LDL a little more. Eggs in moderation are fine for most people. A Mediterranean or DASH pattern overall covers it.
evidence: Replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat is the single highest-evidence lever for LDL (2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline; Cochrane 2020).
Saturated fat under 10 percent of calories for the general population; under 6 percent is the AHA target for people needing to lower LDL.
Soluble fiber 5 to 10 g/day lowers LDL modestly. Plant sterols/stanols 2 g/day lower LDL about 8 to 10 percent.
PREDIMED (NEJM 2018 re-analysis): a Mediterranean pattern with olive oil or nuts reduced major cardiovascular events.
contested: The saturated fat debate is loud online and in the The clinical guideline position has not changed: saturated fat raises LDL, LDL causes atherosclerosis. The app follows the guideline. Coconut oil is not heart-healthy despite marketing.
"Low cholesterol diet" as a term is outdated; dietary cholesterol no longer has a specific numeric limit in US guidance. This module is called heart-healthy / LDL-lowering for that reason.
do_not_claim: Do not call coconut oil heart-healthy.
Do not push plant sterol/stanol products; present them as an option with the evidence.
Do not encode a numeric dietary cholesterol limit; US guidance no longer sets one.
Do not use the term "low cholesterol diet" as the module name.

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG (for the diet as treatment; it is the only treatment).

rules.text: Strict, lifelong avoidance of wheat, barley, rye, and their derivatives (spelt, kamut, farro, durum, semolina, triticale, malt, brewer's yeast from beer).

Hidden gluten: soy sauce, malt vinegar, seasoning blends, processed meats, some medications and supplements, communion wafers, play-dough. The ingredient parser uses a maintained hidden-gluten dictionary.
Regular oats are cross-contaminated with gluten; avoid them.

The 2023 ACG guideline says gluten-free labeled oats are safe for most people with celiac disease; a small subset react to oat avenin. The app allows certified gluten-free oats by default with a toggle to exclude them.
FDA gluten-free labeling rule (21 CFR 101.91): under 20 ppm gluten.

Cross-contact matters: shared fryers, toasters, cutting boards, bulk bins. Recipe and restaurant guidance addresses this, not just ingredients. "Gluten-free" restaurant menus without cross-contact protocols are not celiac-safe; the app distinguishes "celiac-safe" from "gluten-free ingredients."
Steer toward naturally gluten-free whole foods (rice, quinoa, buckwheat, legumes, potatoes, corn) over packaged gluten-free substitutes, which are often low in fiber and fortification.
Newly diagnosed people are often low in iron, folate, B12, vitamin D, calcium, and zinc.
The ACG guideline recommends follow-up with a dietitian experienced in celiac disease.

conflicts.text: Celiac vs low FODMAP: compatible. The FODMAP wheat restriction is about fructans; celiac is about gluten. Certified gluten-free oats are low FODMAP in limited portions (Part D, 6).
Celiac rules stay on in pregnancy.
Celiac disease is a common hidden cause; if iron deficiency is selected without celiac, education mentions screening.

education.plain: A strict, lifelong gluten-free diet is the only treatment for celiac disease. That means no wheat, barley, rye, or their relatives, and watching for hidden gluten in soy sauce, malt vinegar, seasoning blends, processed meats, and some medications. Cross-contact from shared toasters, fryers, and cutting boards matters as much as ingredients. Certified gluten-free oats are safe for most people; regular oats are not. Build meals on naturally gluten-free whole foods like rice, quinoa, buckwheat, beans, potatoes, and corn rather than packaged substitutes, and see a dietitian who knows celiac disease.
evidence: ACG 2023: strict, lifelong gluten avoidance is the treatment; gluten-free labeled oats are safe for most people with celiac disease, with a small subset reacting to oat avenin.
FDA 21 CFR 101.91: foods labeled gluten-free must be under 20 ppm gluten.
Newly diagnosed people are often low in iron, folate, B12, vitamin D, calcium, and zinc; gluten-free processed foods are often low in fiber and fortification.
The ACG guideline recommends follow-up with a dietitian experienced in celiac disease.
contested: Gluten in cosmetics: not a concern unless ingested. Lip products are the only practical concern.
"Gluten-free" restaurant menus without cross-contact protocols are not safe for celiac disease; celiac-safe and gluten-free ingredients are different things.
do_not_claim: Do not treat a "gluten-free" restaurant menu as celiac-safe without cross-contact protocols.
Do not exclude certified gluten-free oats by default; allow them with a toggle.
Do not screen ingredients for gluten using anything other than the maintained dictionary and exact matching; unknown ingredients are reported as not recognized.

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG (mechanism and management are well established).

rules.text: Lactose intolerance is dose-dependent, not an allergy. Most people with lactose malabsorption tolerate about 12 g of lactose (one cup of milk) in a single dose, especially with a meal, and more spread across the day. The app does not default to total dairy elimination.
rules.engine_note: No lactose nutrient key exists in Phase 2 4.3; enforced through lactose-high/lactose-low tags and portion notes.

rules.text: Better tolerated: hard aged cheeses (near zero lactose), yogurt with live cultures, butter, lactose-free milk, lactase enzyme tablets.
Higher lactose: milk, ice cream, soft cheeses, cream, milk-based sauces, whey-based products, some protein powders. Limit by dose rather than eliminating.
Hidden lactose: bread, processed meats, salad dressings, instant potatoes, some medications (as filler).
Calcium and vitamin D adequacy must be maintained. The app counts fortified alternatives and non-dairy calcium sources.

conflicts.text: Lactose is the D in FODMAP. If both are selected, the FODMAP rules cover lactose (Part D, 7).
Lactose intolerance is distinct from cow's milk protein allergy, which is a hard exclusion of all dairy under food allergies.

education.plain: Lactose intolerance is about dose, not all-or-nothing. Most people handle about 12 g of lactose at a time, roughly a cup of milk, especially with food, and more if it is spread across the day. Hard aged cheeses, live-culture yogurt, butter, and lactose-free milk are well tolerated; milk, ice cream, soft cheeses, and cream carry the most lactose. Keep your calcium and vitamin D up with fortified alternatives and non-dairy sources.
evidence: NIH 2010 consensus: lactose intolerance is a dose-dependent intolerance, not an allergy; most people with malabsorption tolerate about 12 g in a single dose.
Hard aged cheeses are near zero lactose; yogurt with live cultures, butter, lactose-free milk, and lactase tablets are better tolerated.
Calcium and vitamin D adequacy must be maintained when dairy is reduced.
contested: Self-diagnosed lactose intolerance is often actually IBS or another issue. A hydrogen breath test confirms it.
Total dairy avoidance is a preference choice, not a medical necessity for most people with lactose intolerance. Medical avoidance and preference avoidance are kept separate in settings.
do_not_claim: Do not default to total dairy elimination.
Do not treat lactose intolerance as a milk allergy; cow's milk protein allergy is handled under food allergies as a hard exclusion.

modules.name: IBS (low FODMAP protocol)
merges: Part B, 15: Low FODMAP. Same three-phase structure. The app does not allow a user to select low FODMAP as a permanent lifestyle without going through reintroduction prompts.

evidence.summary: Rating: MODERATE to STRONG for short-term symptom relief; MODERATE for the full three-phase protocol.

modules.data_note: FODMAP tags are built from published studies and USDA data and are not Monash-verified (Phase 1 stage note).

rules.text: Elimination, 2 to 6 weeks: restrict high-FODMAP foods (oligosaccharides: wheat, rye, onion, garlic, legumes; disaccharides: lactose; monosaccharides: excess fructose in honey, apples, mango, high-fructose corn syrup; polyols: sorbitol, mannitol, stone fruits, sugar-free gum).

Portion size determines FODMAP load. Many foods are low FODMAP at small portions and high at large portions. This app does not encode those portion thresholds: a food tagged high FODMAP is treated as high at any amount, which is the cautious reading. The Monash University FODMAP Diet app carries the tested portion sizes.
Reintroduction, 6 to 8 weeks: systematically test each FODMAP subgroup to identify personal triggers.
Personalization: the long-term diet includes everything tolerated.
The AGA update and ACG guideline both say the diet should be delivered with dietitian support. Long-term elimination without reintroduction harms the microbiome and nutrition.

First-line IBS advice (regular meals; limit alcohol, caffeine, fat, and gas-producing foods; soluble fiber; peppermint oil) has a lower evidence bar than low FODMAP but is simpler. Some guidelines recommend it before low FODMAP.
FODMAP food data in this app comes from published studies and USDA data. It is not Monash-verified.

conflicts.text: Gut-health fiber and fermented-food advice conflicts with low FODMAP elimination (many prebiotic foods are high FODMAP). The app states this, time-limits the elimination phase, and restores fiber and fermented foods during reintroduction (Part D, 3).
FODMAP rules subsume lactose rules (Part D, 7).
Compatible; the FODMAP wheat restriction is about fructans, not gluten. Certified gluten-free oats are low FODMAP in limited portions (Part D, 6).
Running two elimination protocols at once increases restriction load; both are time-limited and count toward the restriction-load check-in.
Pregnancy mode disables every elimination protocol except allergen and celiac rules.
Low FODMAP can help coexisting IBS symptoms in IBD patients in remission (limited evidence). It is presented that way, not as an IBD treatment.

education.plain: Low FODMAP is a three-step process, not a permanent diet. First you cut high-FODMAP foods for 2 to 6 weeks. Then you spend 6 to 8 weeks adding each group back one at a time to learn which ones actually bother you. Then you eat everything you tolerate. Portion size matters: many foods are fine in small amounts and a problem in large ones. Doing this with a dietitian works best, and staying in the elimination phase long-term hurts your gut bacteria and your nutrition.
evidence: ACG 2021: conditional recommendation for a limited trial of a low FODMAP diet. Halmos et al. (Gastroenterology 2014) is the key RCT.
About 50 to 75 percent of people with IBS get meaningful relief. Not everyone.
The three phases are elimination (2 to 6 weeks), reintroduction (6 to 8 weeks), and personalization; the app enforces all three.
Portion size determines FODMAP load; the database carries serving-size thresholds.
contested: Evidence for the reintroduction and personalization phases is thinner than for elimination.
Monash's food data is proprietary; this app's FODMAP tags come from published studies and USDA data and are not Monash-verified.

First-line IBS advice (regular meals, limiting alcohol, caffeine, fat, and gas-producing foods, soluble fiber, peppermint oil) has a lower evidence bar but is simpler; some guidelines recommend it first.
do_not_claim: Do not allow low FODMAP as a permanent lifestyle without reintroduction prompts.
Do not treat FODMAP status as binary allowed/avoid; it depends on portion.
Do not present the FODMAP food data as Monash-verified.
Do not claim everyone with IBS will get relief.

evidence.summary: Rating: LIMITED (expert consensus and a 2025 AGA practice update; little controlled trial evidence).

rules.text: Time-limited low-histamine diagnostic trial (4 to 6 weeks), followed by reintroduction. Triggers commonly reported by patients: alcohol, aged and fermented foods, cured meats, shellfish, tomatoes, spinach, citrus, chocolate, nuts, spicy foods, food additives. These are patient-reported and clinician-observed patterns, not RCT-confirmed. Food lists vary.
Emphasize freshness and cooking method: fresh over leftovers, frozen fish over aged, boiling and steaming over long braising and fermenting. These have the clearest food-chemistry basis.
Reintroduction after the trial: the goal is to find your personal triggers, not to stay restricted forever. Same architecture as low FODMAP.
Symptom tracking tied to meals is the highest-value feature for this population.

The 2025 AGA update says low-histamine, low-FODMAP, gluten-free, and dairy-free elimination diets can be considered for GI symptoms when MCAS is suspected, delivered with nutrition counseling to avoid the harms of restrictive eating. That is permissive language, not a recommendation.

Histamine intolerance (a DAO enzyme problem) and MCAS (abnormal mast cell mediator release) are different conditions. Someone with MCAS may not react to dietary histamine at all, because their symptoms are driven by other mediators (tryptase, prostaglandins, leukotrienes).

conflicts.text: Many low-histamine avoid foods are healthy, high-nutrient foods (spinach, tomatoes, fermented foods, citrus, nuts, fish, olive oil, legumes). Long-term restriction conflicts with heart-health. The time limit plus explicit acknowledgment is the safeguard (Part D, 4).
Fermented foods and many high-fiber foods are excluded during the low-histamine trial. Time-limit the elimination and restore during reintroduction (Part D, 3).
Long-term low-histamine restriction conflicts with diabetes eating patterns; the time limit is the safeguard.
The Mediterranean pattern relies on foods the low-histamine list excludes; time limit plus acknowledgment.
Two elimination protocols at once increase restriction load; both count toward the restriction-load check-in.
Pregnancy mode disables every elimination protocol except allergen and celiac rules.

education.plain: Doctors who treat MCAS often suggest a few weeks on a low-histamine diet to see if it helps. There are no large trials proving it works, and the food lists disagree with each other. Freshness and cooking method matter most: fresh over leftovers, frozen fish over aged, boiling and steaming over long braising and fermenting. The trial lasts 4 to 6 weeks, then you add foods back to find your own triggers. Tracking symptoms against meals is the most useful thing you can do.
education.app_language: Doctors who treat MCAS often suggest trying a low-histamine diet for a few weeks to see if it helps. There are no large clinical trials proving it works, and food lists vary. The goal is to find your personal triggers, not to stay restricted forever.
evidence: The 2025 AGA update says low-histamine, low-FODMAP, gluten-free, and dairy-free elimination diets "can be considered" for GI symptoms when MCAS is suspected, delivered with nutrition counseling. That is the strongest professional-society language available, and it is permissive, not a recommendation.
Histamine intolerance and MCAS are different conditions that get conflated; someone with MCAS may not react to dietary histamine at all.

Only one systematic review has examined restrictive low-histamine diets in mastocytosis and found no clinical trial evidence of a histamine-release mechanism in foods; the support is in vitro and animal data.
Food histamine content varies enormously by freshness, storage, fermentation, and cooking method. Published food lists disagree with each other.

Commonly reported triggers (alcohol, aged and fermented foods, cured meats, shellfish, tomatoes, spinach, citrus, chocolate, nuts, spicy foods, food additives) are patient-reported and clinician-observed, not RCT-confirmed.
contested: Two competing sets of MCAS diagnostic criteria exist (Valent et al., 2019 and 2020 variants).
The SIGHI list is the most widely used practical list but is not peer-reviewed.
do_not_claim: Do not include DAO supplement recommendations.
Do not make "mast cell stabilizing foods" claims (quercetin, luteolin, vitamin C megadoses); the evidence is preclinical and this crosses into supplement marketing.
Do not present the low-histamine diet as a permanent diet or as proven treatment.
Do not conflate histamine intolerance with MCAS.

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG for cardiovascular outcomes and metabolic markers; MODERATE for inflammatory biomarkers; LIMITED for specific inflammatory diseases.

rules.text: Extra virgin olive oil as the main fat.
Daily vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts.
Fish and seafood at least twice a week. Omega-3 from fish (EPA/DHA) has the best data.
rules.why: Omega-3 fats from fish (EPA and DHA) have the best data within the pattern.

rules.text: Moderate poultry, eggs, dairy.
Limited red and processed meat, sweets, and refined grains; minimal ultra-processed food.
Spices like turmeric and ginger have mechanistic and small-trial data, not outcome data. Fine to include as foods; the app makes no health claims about them.

conflicts.text: The low-histamine trial excludes many Mediterranean staples (tomatoes, citrus, nuts, fish, fermented foods). Resolved by the elimination time limit plus acknowledgment (Part D, 4).
High-oxalate foods (spinach, nuts, beets) overlap the plant-forward list; reconcile by pairing with calcium rather than eliminating.
Gastroparesis texture rules win over nut and whole-grain advice.

education.plain: The evidence-based version of an anti-inflammatory diet is the Mediterranean pattern: olive oil as your main fat, vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, and nuts every day, fish at least twice a week, moderate poultry, eggs, and dairy, and not much red or processed meat, sweets, refined grains, or ultra-processed food. It earns its reputation from heart outcomes, not from a dramatic effect on inflammation markers. Turmeric and ginger are fine as foods; they are not medicine.
evidence: PREDIMED (NEJM 2018 corrected re-analysis): Mediterranean diet with olive oil or nuts reduced major cardiovascular events about 30 percent.
Cochrane 2019 (Rees et al.) reviews Mediterranean-style diet for primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
Omega-3 from fish (EPA/DHA) has the best data. Fish oil supplements for the general population: mixed.
The Dietary Inflammatory Index literature is observational and supplies the concept only.
contested: "Anti-inflammatory diet" as marketed online (nightshade avoidance, lectin avoidance, dairy elimination, "alkaline" foods) is not evidence-based.
Whether the diet lowers CRP and IL-6 meaningfully in healthy people is modest and inconsistent. The cardiovascular outcome data is what justifies the pattern.
do_not_claim: Do not encode nightshade avoidance, lectin avoidance, dairy elimination, or "alkaline" foods.
Do not recommend fish oil supplements for the general population.
Do not make health claims about turmeric, ginger, or other spices.
Do not claim the pattern treats specific inflammatory diseases.

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG.

rules.text: Added sugar under 25 g/day (6 tsp) for women (AHA).
rules.why: The target is added sugar, not the sugar naturally in fruit or in plain milk and yogurt.

rules.text: Added sugar under 36 g/day (9 tsp) for men (AHA).
rules.why: The target is added sugar, not the sugar naturally in fruit or in plain milk and yogurt.

rules.text: Free sugars under 10 percent of calories, ideally under 5 percent (WHO 2015).
rules.why: The target is added sugar, not the sugar naturally in fruit or in plain milk and yogurt.

rules.text: Target added sugar, not total sugar. Fruit and plain dairy sugars are not the concern.
Sugar-sweetened beverages are the largest source and the first thing to cut.
Read the Added Sugars line on labels. Sugar has 60-plus label names (dextrose, maltose, cane juice, agave, rice syrup, fruit juice concentrate); the ingredient parser carries this dictionary.

Non-nutritive sweeteners: the WHO 2023 guideline advises against using them for weight control, based on long-term observational data; short-term use as a bridge is acceptable. Both positions are presented.

education.plain: The target is added sugar, not the sugar naturally in fruit or plain milk and yogurt. The AHA limit is under 25 g a day for women and 36 g for men; WHO says under 10 percent of calories, ideally under 5. Sugary drinks are the biggest source and the first thing to cut. Check the Added Sugars line on the label, and know that sugar hides under 60-plus names in ingredient lists.
evidence: AHA Scientific Statement (Johnson et al., Circulation 2009): women under 25 g/day (6 tsp), men under 36 g/day (9 tsp).
WHO 2015: under 10 percent of calories, ideally under 5 percent.
FDA's 2016 label rule added an Added Sugars line.
contested: Non-nutritive sweeteners: WHO 2023 advises against them for weight control based on long-term observational data; short-term use as a bridge is acceptable.
do_not_claim: Do not target total sugar or flag fruit and plain dairy sugars.
Do not present non-nutritive sweeteners as a weight-control tool.

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG for confirmed soy allergy (avoidance is the treatment); preference otherwise.

rules.text: For a confirmed soy allergy, select soy under Food allergies. That is a hard exclusion with no override: soybeans, edamame, tofu, tempeh, miso, natto, soy milk, soy protein isolate, textured vegetable protein, soy flour, most soy sauce (which also contains wheat).
Preference soy avoidance (soft exclusion, can be overridden). The evidence does not support harm from soy foods in normal amounts.
Hidden soy: vegetable broth, baked goods, processed meats, protein bars, Asian sauces, vegetarian meat substitutes, some peanut butters, "natural flavors" in some products.

Highly refined soybean oil is exempt from allergen labeling and is tolerated by most people with soy allergy; soy lecithin is usually tolerated. Allergist-dependent: the app defaults to excluding both for allergy and lets you (with allergist input) relax it.

conflicts.text: Soy avoidance narrows the plant-protein base. The app surfaces alternative proteins: legumes other than soy, seitan if no gluten issue, eggs and dairy if permitted, quinoa, hemp (Part D, 8).

education.plain: If you have a diagnosed soy allergy, set it under Food allergies so it becomes a hard exclusion covering soybeans, edamame, tofu, tempeh, miso, soy milk, soy protein, and most soy sauce. Soy hides in broth, baked goods, processed meats, protein bars, and sauces. Highly refined soybean oil and soy lecithin are tolerated by most people with soy allergy; ask your allergist. If you avoid soy for other reasons, that is a preference, and the evidence does not show harm from soy foods in normal amounts.
evidence: AAAAI/ACAAI practice parameters and NIAID guidelines: avoidance is the treatment for confirmed food allergy.
FDA FALCPA: soy is a major allergen labeled "Contains: Soy"; highly refined soybean oil is exempt from labeling and tolerated by most people with soy allergy; soy lecithin is usually tolerated.
contested: Preference soy avoidance (hormone concerns, GMO concerns): the evidence does not support harm from soy foods in normal amounts. Filed under preference with a neutral explainer.
do_not_claim: Do not present soy foods in normal amounts as harmful.
Do not treat preference soy avoidance as a medical rule.

evidence.summary: Rating: MODERATE for fiber and dietary diversity; LIMITED for fermented foods and specific probiotic foods; INSUFFICIENT for most "gut health" product claims.

rules.text: Fiber 25 to 38 g/day depending on sex and age (Institute of Medicine), from a variety of whole plant foods. Increase gradually with fluid.
rules.why: Reynolds et al. found that eating 25 to 29 g of fiber a day was associated with a 15 to 30 percent lower risk of all-cause and cardiovascular death, and lower rates of type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer.

rules.text: Plant diversity: aim for a wide range of plant foods weekly. The "30 plants" idea is a reasonable heuristic from observational data, not a proven target.
Fermented foods with live cultures (yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi): small RCT support, generally recommended.
Limit ultra-processed foods, added sugars, and excess alcohol.
Probiotic supplements are not recommended by the AGA for general gut health. The app does not recommend them.

conflicts.text: Gut health prescriptions conflict with the low FODMAP elimination phase. The conflict logic time-limits that phase and restores fiber and fermented foods during reintroduction (Part D, 3).
Gut health prescriptions conflict with the low-histamine elimination phase. Time-limited, then restored (Part D, 3).
Gastroparesis rules win on texture; meet fiber goals through soluble, cooked, or blended sources where possible.
High-oxalate plant foods overlap the gut-health list; pair with calcium rather than eliminating.
During an IBD flare, low-fiber or low-residue eating is temporary and overrides the fiber target; in remission adequate fiber is part of the IBD pattern.
Diarrhea during treatment calls for low fiber temporarily; constipation calls for more. Symptom-driven.

education.plain: The best-supported things you can do for your gut are eat 25 to 38 grams of fiber a day from a wide variety of plant foods, add it gradually with plenty of fluid, include some live-culture fermented foods like yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, or kimchi, and cut back on ultra-processed food, added sugar, and excess alcohol. Probiotic supplements are not recommended for general gut health, and microbiome test kits are not clinically validated.
evidence: Reynolds et al. (Lancet 2019, commissioned by WHO): 25 to 29 g/day of fiber associated with 15 to 30 percent lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, and lower incidence of T2D and colorectal cancer.
Wastyk et al. (Cell 2021): fermented food intake increased microbiome diversity and lowered inflammatory markers in a 10 week RCT, n=36. Small but well designed.
American Gut Project (mSystems 2018): people eating 30-plus plant types per week had more diverse microbiomes. Observational.
AGA 2020 (Su et al.): does not recommend probiotics for most GI conditions outside specific narrow uses.
contested: Microbiome testing kits and personalized microbiome diets are not clinically validated.
The "30 plants" target is a heuristic from observational data, not a proven target.
do_not_claim: Do not recommend probiotic supplements for general gut health.
Do not present microbiome testing kits or personalized microbiome diets as validated.
Do not present "30 plants a week" as a proven target.
Do not make "gut health" product claims.

modules.name: Food allergies
modules.phase1_ref: Part C (Food allergies); Part B, 13; Addendum 2, D10 (caregiver mode)

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG (avoidance is the treatment for confirmed food allergy; Part B 13 and Part C). Hard exclusions with no override.

rules.text: Milk: hard exclusion, no override. Cow's milk protein allergy excludes all dairy (distinct from lactose intolerance).
Egg: hard exclusion, no override.
Fish: hard exclusion, no override.
Crustacean shellfish: hard exclusion, no override.
Tree nuts: hard exclusion, no override.
Peanuts: hard exclusion, no override.
Wheat: hard exclusion, no override.

Soybeans: hard exclusion, no override (soybeans, edamame, tofu, tempeh, miso, natto, soy milk, soy protein isolate, textured vegetable protein, soy flour, most soy sauce). Refined soybean oil and soy lecithin are excluded by default and can be relaxed only with allergist input (see soy-free module).

Soy allergy: refined soybean oil and soy lecithin are not allowed unless your allergist says they are fine. Highly refined soybean oil is exempt from allergen labeling; soy lecithin is not, and labels declare it as soy. Most people with a soy allergy tolerate both, which is why the choice is yours to make with your allergist.
Sesame (ninth major allergen under the FASTER Act): hard exclusion, no override.
Custom allergen entries beyond the nine FDA major allergens are also hard exclusions with no override.
"May contain" and shared-facility labels are user-configurable. Many people with allergies avoid these; the evidence on actual risk is mixed.

The ingredient parser and recipe screener are safety-critical. They never rely on a language model. An unrecognized ingredient is reported as not recognized and never counted as safe when an allergen is selected.

conflicts.text: Soy allergy plus plant-based or vegan preferences reduces protein options; the app surfaces alternative proteins (legumes other than soy, seitan if no gluten issue, eggs and dairy if permitted, quinoa, hemp) (Part D, 8).
Milk allergy is a hard exclusion of all dairy; lactose intolerance is dose-dependent. They are different settings.
Allergen rules stay on in pregnancy.

caregiver_mode.note: Caregiver mode lets an adult account holder manage a child's diagnosed food allergies. Hard age gate on the account holder; pediatrician-reviewed content (D10).

education.plain: Food allergens are the one thing in this app that nothing can override. Milk, egg, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soy, and sesame are the nine FDA major allergens, and you can add your own. Whether you also avoid "may contain" and shared-facility foods is your call; many people with allergies do, and the evidence on actual risk is mixed. If the app does not recognize an ingredient, it tells you so rather than assuming it is safe.
evidence: The nine FDA major allergens (FALCPA 2004; sesame added by the FASTER Act 2021): milk, egg, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, sesame.
Avoidance is the treatment for confirmed food allergy (AAAAI/ACAAI practice parameters, NIAID guidelines).
Highly refined soybean oil is exempt from allergen labeling and tolerated by most people with soy allergy; soy lecithin is usually tolerated.
contested: "May contain" and shared-facility labels: many people with allergies avoid these; the evidence on actual risk is mixed.
do_not_claim: No setting, preference, mode, or acknowledgment can override an allergen exclusion.
The allergen path must never rely on an LLM alone; unknown ingredients are never counted as safe.
A confirmed allergen slipping through is the single worst failure the app can have.

evidence.summary: Info only. Derived automatically from selected conditions; each avoidance carries the rating of the module it came from.

rules.text: Medical avoidances are derived automatically from your selected conditions. You can see and annotate them but cannot remove one without acknowledging the condition rule it comes from.
Medical avoidance and preference avoidance are kept separate in settings. Example: total dairy avoidance is a preference for most people with lactose intolerance, not a medical necessity.

education.plain: Medical avoidances are the foods the app steers you away from because of a condition you selected. You can read why each one is there and add your own notes, but removing one means acknowledging the condition rule behind it.
evidence: Derived from the condition modules; see each module's citations.
do_not_claim: Do not let a medical avoidance be removed silently; removal requires acknowledging the condition rule.

evidence.summary: Info only. Free-form, soft exclusions the user can override at any time. Religious and ethical patterns (halal, kosher, vegetarian, vegan) are pre-built options.

prebuilt_options.label: Halal
prebuilt_options.note: Pre-built preference option. Phase 1 gives no food rules for halal; it is a soft, user-defined exclusion set.

prebuilt_options.label: Kosher
prebuilt_options.note: Pre-built preference option. Phase 1 gives no food rules for kosher; it is a soft, user-defined exclusion set.

prebuilt_options.label: Vegan

Religious and ethical patterns (halal, kosher, vegetarian, vegan) are pre-built options. Vegetarian and vegan carry nutrition rules in the vegetarian-vegan module.

evidence: Part C: religious and ethical patterns belong under preferences as pre-built options.
do_not_claim: Do not treat a preference avoidance as a medical rule or an allergen.

modules.name: Weight management / obesity, including GLP-1 medications

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG that a sustained calorie deficit produces weight loss; MODERATE for any one diet composition being superior; LIMITED (consensus-based) for GLP-1-specific nutrition guidance.

rules.text: A 500 to 750 kcal/day deficit, or an eating pattern that produces one, is the mechanism. The pattern you will stick to is the right one; Mediterranean, DASH, low-carb, and plant-based all work when calories are controlled.
rules.engine_note: A calorie deficit needs an energy-needs estimate the app does not make; shown as a habit, not enforced as a number.

rules.text: 5 to 10 percent weight loss is the clinically meaningful target.
GLP-1 users: smaller meals, protein first at each meal, adequate fluids, fiber for constipation; avoid high-fat and very large meals (nausea); screen for undereating.

Higher protein and resistance training to protect muscle and bone during rapid loss: about 80 to 120 g of protein a day. The joint GLP-1 advisory offers this fixed daily target because per-kilogram targets based on actual body weight can overstate needs in people with obesity. Higher targets, such as 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg/day, have also been proposed during active loss.
rules.why: Protect muscle and bone during fast loss with higher protein, about 80 to 120 g a day, plus resistance exercise.
rules.engine_note: Until September 30, 2026 this was 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg/day times actual body weight, flagged VERIFY. The advisory reports that range as proposed by others and offers 80 to 120 g/day as its practical target (VERIFY-log A26).

rules.text: Micronutrient adequacy during GLP-1 therapy: iron, B12, vitamin D, calcium, folate are the ones flagged.
Both GLP-1 documents call for baseline screening for disordered eating before starting therapy. The app does not do this screening; ask your prescriber about it.
Weight regain after stopping GLP-1s is the norm; maintenance-phase content matters more than loss-phase content.

conflicts.text: GLP-1 higher-protein guidance conflicts with CKD protein limits. Clinician-set protein target required if both are selected.
Pregnancy disables weight-loss features. Weight gain by pre-pregnancy BMI category, not weight loss.
During active cancer treatment, preventing weight and muscle loss is the priority, often the opposite of a calorie deficit. Clinician decides.
PCOS weight-loss guidance applies only if overweight; the app does not push calorie restriction to PCOS users who are not overweight.

education.plain: Weight loss comes from a sustained calorie deficit of about 500 to 750 kcal a day, and the diet you can actually keep is the right one; low-fat and low-carb came out the same at 12 months in DIETFITS. Losing 5 to 10 percent of your weight is the meaningful target. If you take a GLP-1 medication, eat smaller meals, put protein first, drink enough, get fiber for constipation, avoid very large or fatty meals, and watch for eating too little. Protect muscle with higher protein, about 80 to 120 g a day, and resistance training. Most people regain weight after stopping a GLP-1, so the maintenance plan matters more than the loss plan.
evidence: 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS guideline: a 500 to 750 kcal/day deficit produces weight loss; 5 to 10 percent loss is clinically meaningful.
DIETFITS (JAMA 2018): no difference between healthy low-fat and healthy low-carb at 12 months.

GLP-1 joint advisory (AJCN 2025) and Sievenpiper consensus (Obesity Pillars 2026): smaller meals, protein first, fluids, fiber, avoid high-fat and very large meals, screen for undereating; higher protein and resistance training to protect muscle and bone (the advisory offers an absolute 80 to 120 g of protein a day); iron, B12, vitamin D, calcium, folate flagged.
Both GLP-1 documents call for baseline screening for disordered eating.
contested: This is the only area where calories are unavoidably central; calories appear only where the experts recommend, and here they do.

The AJCN GLP-1 advisory drew published letters criticizing it for calling itself evidence-based when much of it is extrapolated; the authors acknowledge the evidence gap. The Sievenpiper consensus is primarily indirect evidence.

Protein: the AJCN advisory says 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg/day has been proposed during active weight loss, that it is unclear whether goals for people with obesity should use actual or adjusted weight because actual weight can significantly overestimate needs, and that an absolute target of 80 to 120 g a day may help adherence while ensuring adequate intake. The app uses 80 to 120 g a day.
Meal replacements and very-low-calorie diets: legitimate under supervision, not a consumer-app feature.
do_not_claim: Do not offer meal replacements or very-low-calorie diets.
Do not turn on calorie targets or weight-loss plans before the eating-disorder screen, or after a positive screen.
Do not claim any one diet composition is superior for weight loss.
Do not present 80 to 120 g of protein a day as trial-tested: it is the advisory's practical target, drawn largely from indirect evidence.

variants.label: Weight loss (with or without a GLP-1)
Taking a GLP-1; not focused on weight loss

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG for sodium restriction; MODERATE for protein restriction; potassium and phosphorus are INDIVIDUALIZED by lab values and must not be set by the app.

tier2.label: Potassium limit (clinician-set)
tier2.consensus: No blanket restriction. Restrict only when serum potassium is high; the level of restriction depends on labs and medications.
tier2.why: The app never sets a potassium limit. Enter the target your nephrologist or renal dietitian gave you, or the app runs in sodium-and-protein-only mode with a clear statement that potassium was not applied.

tier2.label: Phosphorus limit (clinician-set)
tier2.consensus: Prioritize avoiding phosphate additives over restricting natural phosphorus in plant foods; any numeric limit is set by labs.
tier2.why: The app never sets a phosphorus limit. Enter the target your nephrologist or renal dietitian gave you, or the app runs in sodium-and-protein-only mode with a clear statement that phosphorus was not applied.

tier2.label: Protein target (clinician-set when combined with other protein rules)
tier2.when: module higher-protein-older-adult or weight-management-glp1 or dialysis or cancer-nutrition or kidney-stones
tier2.consensus: 0.8 g/kg/day for CKD stages 3 to 5 not on dialysis (KDIGO 2024); supervised low-protein 0.55 to 0.60 g/kg for metabolically stable patients (KDOQI 2020); 0.8 g/kg with diabetes; avoid above 1.3 g/kg.
tier2.why: CKD protein limits conflict with high-protein patterns and GLP-1 protein guidance. A clinician-set protein target is required if both are selected.

rules.text: Sodium under 2,300 mg/day (KDOQI; KDIGO both under 2 g sodium).
rules.why: Diet matters because the kidneys clear sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and the waste from protein; when they work less well, those can build up.

rules.text: Protein: KDIGO 2024 recommends 0.8 g/kg/day for adults with CKD stages 3 to 5 not on dialysis. People with diabetes and CKD: 0.8 g/kg. Avoid high-protein intake above 1.3 g/kg. Tier 1 on its own; becomes clinician-set when combined with another protein rule.
rules.why: Diet matters because the kidneys clear sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and the waste from protein; when they work less well, those can build up.

rules.text: KDOQI 2020 allows a supervised low-protein diet of 0.55 to 0.60 g/kg for metabolically stable patients. Supervised only; the app does not choose this level.
Avoid high-protein intake above 1.3 g/kg/day.
rules.why: Diet matters because the kidneys clear sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and the waste from protein; when they work less well, those can build up.

rules.text: Potassium: no blanket restriction. Restrict only when serum potassium is high; the level depends on labs and medications. Plant potassium is less bioavailable than animal or additive potassium, and plant-forward patterns are now encouraged in CKD. Enter the limit your clinician gave you.
rules.why: Diet matters because the kidneys clear sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and the waste from protein; when they work less well, those can build up.

rules.text: Additive potassium (including potassium-based salt substitutes) is more bioavailable than plant potassium; the hypertension salt-substitute suggestion does not apply in CKD.
Phosphorus: any numeric limit comes from your nephrologist or renal dietitian. The app does not set one.
rules.why: Diet matters because the kidneys clear sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and the waste from protein; when they work less well, those can build up.

rules.text: Prioritize avoiding phosphate additives (processed foods, colas, "phos" ingredients) over restricting natural phosphorus in plant foods.
Mediterranean and plant-forward patterns are associated with slower progression (observational).
All nutrient values come from USDA FoodData Central and deterministic math, never from a language model estimate. Published LLM studies show models get sodium, potassium, and phosphorus wrong.
Without clinician-entered potassium and phosphorus targets, the app operates in sodium-and-protein-only mode with a clear statement that potassium and phosphorus were not applied.

conflicts.text: Hard conflict with the hypertension potassium recommendation (3,500 to 5,000 mg). CKD wins; the app suppresses the potassium target and says why.
Heart failure carries the same potassium-medication screen as hypertension; CKD suppresses any potassium encouragement. Inferred from A2 and A8.
Conflict with high-protein patterns. Clinician-set protein target required if both are selected.
Conflict with GLP-1 protein guidance. Clinician-set protein target required if both are selected.
Dialysis (stage 5D) has different rules entirely. Do not run both; the dialysis module replaces this one.
Kidney stones plus CKD: fluid and protein rules interact; clinician-set.
Kidney disease is on the low-carb/ketogenic caution list; clinician decision.
Cancer-treatment protein (1.0 to 1.5 g/kg) exceeds the CKD ceiling; both are clinician-set.
The osteoporosis protein target follows A12 and inherits its CKD conflict: clinician-set.

education.plain: For kidney disease before dialysis, the app applies two things on its own: sodium under 2,300 mg a day and protein around 0.8 g per kilogram of body weight, never above 1.3. Potassium and phosphorus depend on your labs, so the app will not set them; enter the numbers your nephrologist or renal dietitian gave you, or the app runs in sodium-and-protein-only mode and says so. Avoid phosphate additives in processed foods and colas before worrying about phosphorus in plant foods. Plant-forward eating is encouraged.
evidence: KDIGO 2024 and KDOQI 2020: sodium under 2 g/day (under 2,300 mg).

KDIGO 2024: protein 0.8 g/kg/day for CKD stages 3 to 5 not on dialysis; KDOQI 2020 allows a supervised low-protein diet of 0.55 to 0.60 g/kg for metabolically stable patients; 0.8 g/kg with diabetes; avoid above 1.3 g/kg.
Potassium: no blanket restriction; restrict only when serum potassium is high. Plant potassium is less bioavailable than animal or additive potassium.
Phosphorus: prioritize avoiding phosphate additives over restricting natural phosphorus in plant foods.
Mediterranean and plant-forward patterns are associated with slower progression (observational).
contested: This is the highest-risk module in the app after allergens. Published LLM studies show models get sodium, potassium, and phosphorus wrong; every number here comes from USDA data and deterministic math.
do_not_claim: The app never sets a potassium or phosphorus limit.
Do not apply the hypertension potassium target or potassium-based salt substitutes to someone with CKD.
Do not estimate any nutrient value with a language model.
Do not run dialysis (stage 5D) under these rules; it is a separate module.

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG for weight loss as treatment; MODERATE for the Mediterranean pattern; MODERATE for limiting fructose and alcohol.

rules.text: Weight loss of 5 percent reduces liver fat; 7 to 10 percent improves inflammation and fibrosis. This is the treatment.
Mediterranean pattern is the recommended default.
Minimize sugar-sweetened beverages and added fructose (high-fructose corn syrup in particular).
Alcohol: avoid or minimize; abstain if fibrosis is present.
Coffee (2 to 3 cups/day, unsweetened) is associated with lower fibrosis risk. Reasonable to mention, not a prescription.

conflicts.text: Fully compatible with diabetes rules. This condition rarely travels alone.
Fully compatible with lipid rules.
Fully compatible with hypertension rules.

education.plain: For fatty liver disease, weight loss is the treatment: losing 5 percent of your weight reduces liver fat, and 7 to 10 percent improves inflammation and scarring. Eat Mediterranean-style, cut sugary drinks and high-fructose corn syrup, and avoid or minimize alcohol; if you have fibrosis, stop entirely. Unsweetened coffee, 2 to 3 cups a day, is linked to lower fibrosis risk, but it is not a prescription.
evidence: AASLD 2023: weight loss of 5 percent reduces liver fat; 7 to 10 percent improves inflammation and fibrosis.
Mediterranean pattern is the recommended default; minimize sugar-sweetened beverages and added fructose.
Coffee 2 to 3 cups/day, unsweetened, is associated with lower fibrosis risk.
do_not_claim: Do not present coffee as a prescription.
Do not claim the plan treats liver disease; weight loss and the eating pattern support liver health.

evidence.summary: Rating: MODERATE for weight loss and meal timing; LIMITED for specific trigger-food elimination.

rules.text: Weight loss if overweight (the strongest lifestyle lever).
No eating within 2 to 3 hours of lying down. Elevate the head of the bed for nighttime symptoms.
Smaller meals, less fat per meal.

The guideline does not recommend blanket elimination of classic trigger foods (coffee, chocolate, citrus, tomato, spicy, fatty, carbonated, mint, alcohol). It recommends avoiding the ones that trigger you. These are optional toggles with the evidence note, not default exclusions.

education.plain: For reflux, the things with real evidence are losing weight if you carry extra, not eating within 2 to 3 hours of lying down, raising the head of your bed, and eating smaller, lower-fat meals. The classic trigger foods (coffee, chocolate, citrus, tomato, spicy, fatty, fizzy, mint, alcohol) are not banned; the guideline says avoid the ones that bother you. You can turn each one on as a toggle.
evidence: ACG 2022: weight loss if overweight is the strongest lifestyle lever; no eating within 2 to 3 hours of lying down; elevate the head of the bed for nighttime symptoms; smaller meals with less fat.
contested: Trigger-food elimination has limited evidence; the guideline recommends individual avoidance, not blanket elimination.
do_not_claim: Do not exclude classic trigger foods by default.
Do not claim the plan treats reflux.

modules.name: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis)

evidence.summary: Rating: MODERATE for Mediterranean pattern in remission; STRONG for exclusive enteral nutrition in pediatric Crohn's (out of app scope); LIMITED for named diets (Specific Carbohydrate Diet, Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet); INSUFFICIENT for most online IBD diets.

rules.text: In remission: Mediterranean-style diet with adequate fiber. Avoid unnecessary restriction; malnutrition is the bigger risk in IBD.
In remission: limit ultra-processed food, emulsifiers, and added sugar.
During flares or with strictures: low-fiber or low-residue eating, soft cooked vegetables; avoid nuts, seeds, raw vegetables, and skins. Temporary.
During a flare, prefer soft, cooked, small-particle foods.
Lactose intolerance is common in active disease; not a reason for permanent dairy avoidance.
Nutrient risk: iron, B12 (especially after ileal resection), vitamin D, zinc, folate. Refer for labs.
Two modes: remission and flare. You switch modes; the app does not diagnose a flare. Flare mode expires and prompts a check-in.

conflicts.text: Flare mode temporarily overrides the gut-health fiber target; remission restores adequate fiber.
Low FODMAP can help coexisting IBS symptoms in IBD patients in remission (limited evidence). It is presented that way, not as an IBD treatment.

modes.expires_days_note: 14 days is an app default for the check-in prompt, not a clinical number. Phase 1 says only that flare mode expires and prompts a check-in.

education.plain: When your IBD is in remission, eat a Mediterranean-style diet with enough fiber and go easy on ultra-processed food, emulsifiers, and added sugar. Do not restrict more than you need to; malnutrition is the bigger danger. During a flare or if you have a stricture, switch to flare mode: soft cooked vegetables, low fiber, no nuts, seeds, raw vegetables, or skins, and only for as long as needed. You switch the mode; the app does not decide you are flaring. Ask your care team to check iron, B12, vitamin D, zinc, and folate.
evidence: AGA 2024 practice update and IOIBD 2020: Mediterranean-style diet in remission; limit ultra-processed food, emulsifiers, and added sugar; avoid unnecessary restriction.
DINE-CD (Gastroenterology 2021): the Specific Carbohydrate Diet was not superior to a Mediterranean diet in Crohn's disease.
During flares or with strictures: low-fiber or low-residue eating, temporary.
Exclusive enteral nutrition has strong evidence in pediatric Crohn's disease; out of app scope.
contested: Named diets (SCD, Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet) have limited evidence; most online IBD diets have insufficient evidence.
Low FODMAP can help coexisting IBS symptoms in IBD patients in remission (limited evidence).
do_not_claim: Do not encode SCD, low-FODMAP-for-IBD, or "autoimmune protocol" as IBD treatments.
Do not diagnose a flare; the user switches modes.
Do not encourage permanent dairy avoidance because of lactose intolerance in active disease.
Do not leave flare mode on indefinitely; it expires and prompts a check-in.

evidence.summary: Rating: MODERATE for weight loss (if overweight) and general healthy eating; LIMITED for any specific diet composition.

rules.text: No specific diet composition is superior. Healthy eating principles apply, tailored to preference.
If overweight, 5 to 10 percent weight loss improves metabolic, reproductive, and psychological outcomes. The app does not push calorie restriction to PCOS users who are not overweight.
Lower glycemic index and Mediterranean-style patterns have supportive but not decisive evidence for insulin resistance.

The guideline explicitly warns about weight stigma and disordered eating risk in this population. The app does not screen for disordered eating; talk with your clinician before starting any weight-focused plan.

conflicts.text: PCOS weight-loss guidance applies only if overweight; the app does not push calorie restriction to PCOS users who are not overweight.

education.plain: There is no special PCOS diet. Healthy eating principles apply, shaped to what you like. If you carry extra weight, losing 5 to 10 percent improves metabolic, reproductive, and mood outcomes; if you do not, this app will not push calorie restriction on you. Lower glycemic index and Mediterranean-style eating have some support for insulin resistance but nothing decisive. Gluten-free, dairy-free, and the "PCOS diets" sold online have no guideline support.
evidence: International PCOS guideline 2023: no specific diet composition is superior; if overweight, 5 to 10 percent weight loss improves metabolic, reproductive, and psychological outcomes.
Lower glycemic index and Mediterranean-style patterns: supportive but not decisive evidence for insulin resistance.
The guideline explicitly warns about weight stigma and disordered eating risk in this population.
contested: Gluten-free, dairy-free, and "PCOS diets" sold online have no guideline support.
do_not_claim: Do not encode gluten-free, dairy-free, or online "PCOS diets".
Do not push calorie restriction to PCOS users who are not overweight.
Do not turn on weight-focused features without the eating-disorder screen.
