evidence.summary: Rating: MODERATE for calcium and vitamin D; MODERATE for protein; LIMITED for everything else.

rules.text: Calcium 1,000 mg/day (women under 50, men under 70), food first, supplements only to fill the gap.
rules.why: Get 1,000 mg of calcium a day if you are a woman under 50 or a man under 70; 1,200 mg a day if you are a woman 50 or older or a man 70 or older.

rules.text: Calcium 1,200 mg/day (women 50-plus, men 70-plus), food first, supplements only to fill the gap; supplemental calcium above 1,000 mg has cardiovascular questions.
rules.why: Get 1,000 mg of calcium a day if you are a woman under 50 or a man under 70; 1,200 mg a day if you are a woman 50 or older or a man 70 or older.

rules.text: Vitamin D 800 to 1,000 IU/day for adults 50-plus (BHOF); this is a supplement recommendation because food sources are inadequate.
rules.why: Adults 50 and older need 800 to 1,000 IU of vitamin D a day, which usually means a supplement because food does not supply it.

rules.text: Protein adequate (1.0 to 1.2 g/kg for older adults, per A12).
rules.why: The protein target comes from the PROT-AGE group's review of muscle and bone outcomes in people over 65.

rules.text: Limit alcohol; caffeine moderate; sodium moderate (high sodium increases calcium loss).
Fruits and vegetables (potassium, magnesium, vitamin K) are associated with bone density.

conflicts.text: The osteoporosis protein target follows A12 and inherits its CKD conflict: clinician-set.

education.plain: For bone health, aim for 1,000 mg of calcium a day (1,200 if you are a woman over 50 or a man over 70), from food first and supplements only to fill the gap, since supplemental calcium above 1,000 mg raises heart questions. Adults over 50 need 800 to 1,000 IU of vitamin D a day, which usually means a supplement. Get enough protein, about 1.0 to 1.2 g per kilogram, limit alcohol, keep caffeine and sodium moderate, and eat plenty of fruits and vegetables. There are no bone-building superfoods.
evidence: BHOF 2022: calcium 1,000 mg/day (women under 50, men under 70) or 1,200 mg/day (women 50-plus, men 70-plus), food first; vitamin D 800 to 1,000 IU/day for adults 50-plus.
Protein 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg for older adults (per A12).
Fruits and vegetables (potassium, magnesium, vitamin K) are associated with bone density.
contested: Supplemental calcium above 1,000 mg has cardiovascular questions.
do_not_claim: Do not make bone-building "superfood" claims.
Do not push calcium supplements beyond filling the gap from food.

modules.review_note: Engine wiring: calcium targets keyed to sex and age per BHOF; unknown sex or age applies the stricter number.

evidence.summary: Rating: MODERATE for dietary strategies; STRONG that diet alone rarely corrects established deficiency.

rules.text: Heme iron (red meat, poultry, fish) is absorbed 2 to 3 times better than non-heme iron (legumes, fortified grains, leafy greens, tofu).
Pair non-heme iron with vitamin C; separate iron-rich meals from tea, coffee, calcium supplements, and high-calcium foods by 1 to 2 hours.
Cast-iron cookware adds iron modestly.
Diet supports; oral or IV iron treats. The BSG guideline is explicit that established deficiency needs supplementation and a search for the cause (GI blood loss, celiac disease, menstrual loss).
Celiac disease is a common hidden cause of iron deficiency; if you have not been tested, ask about screening.

conflicts.text: Vegetarian and vegan users are at higher risk; the app raises the iron guidance automatically.
Celiac disease is a common hidden cause; if iron deficiency is selected without celiac, education mentions screening.

Keep iron supplements about 4 hours from levothyroxine (the usual advice; the ATA guideline calls the gap untested). The thyroid timing rule shows this on the Plan; the app does not move meals on the clock.

education.plain: Food helps with iron, but established iron deficiency needs iron supplements, oral or IV, and a doctor looking for the cause, such as gut blood loss, celiac disease, or heavy periods. Heme iron from red meat, poultry, and fish is absorbed 2 to 3 times better than plant iron. Pair plant iron with vitamin C, and keep iron-rich meals 1 to 2 hours away from tea, coffee, calcium supplements, and high-calcium foods. Cast-iron pans add a little.
evidence: BSG 2021: established deficiency needs supplementation and a search for the cause (GI blood loss, celiac disease, menstrual loss).
Heme iron is absorbed 2 to 3 times better than non-heme iron; pair non-heme iron with vitamin C; separate from tea, coffee, calcium supplements, and high-calcium foods by 1 to 2 hours.
Cast-iron cookware adds iron modestly.
do_not_claim: Do not claim diet alone corrects established iron deficiency.
Do not skip the cause-finding message; celiac disease is a common hidden cause.

evidence.summary: Rating: MODERATE for the small-particle diet; MODERATE for low fat, low fiber, small frequent meals.

rules.text: Small-particle diet: foods that are easy to mash with a fork; avoid fibrous, tough, or large-particle foods (raw vegetables, whole nuts, seeds, skins, tough meat).
Prefer soft, mashable, blended, or liquid foods; liquids and blended meals empty faster.
Low fat (fat slows emptying), except liquid fats are often tolerated.
Low fiber, especially insoluble fiber; avoid bezoar-forming foods (persimmons, orange membranes, celery).
Small, frequent meals (4 to 6/day).
Sit upright after eating; walking after meals helps.
Nutrient adequacy is the risk; a multivitamin is often needed.

conflicts.text: Conflicts directly with gut-health fiber advice. Gastroparesis rules win on texture; meet fiber goals through soluble, cooked, or blended sources where possible.
Conflicts with diabetes fiber advice; texture wins, fiber from soluble, cooked, or blended sources. Gastroparesis is common in long-standing diabetes (glucose control affects emptying).
Conflicts with heart-healthy nut and whole-grain advice; texture wins.
Whole nuts and raw vegetables give way to texture rules.

education.plain: With gastroparesis, choose foods you could mash with a fork and skip raw vegetables, whole nuts, seeds, skins, and tough meat. Keep fat low, though liquid fats are usually fine, and keep fiber low, especially the rough insoluble kind; avoid persimmons, orange membranes, and celery, which can form bezoars. Eat 4 to 6 small meals a day; liquids and blended meals leave the stomach faster. Sit up after eating and take a walk. Because this diet is narrow, a multivitamin is often needed.
evidence: ACG 2022 and Olausson et al. (RCT, 2014): small-particle diet reduces symptoms in diabetic gastroparesis.
Low fat (fat slows emptying) except liquid fats; low fiber, especially insoluble; small, frequent meals (4 to 6/day); liquids and blended meals empty faster.
Sit upright after eating; walking after meals helps.
do_not_claim: Do not let fiber or nut advice from other modules override the texture rules; gastroparesis wins on texture.
Do not claim the diet treats gastroparesis; it manages symptoms.

evidence.summary: Rating: MODERATE for medication-timing rules; LIMITED for everything else; INSUFFICIENT for "thyroid diets".

rules.text: Levothyroxine: take it the same way every day, with water on an empty stomach, either 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime, 3 or more hours after the evening meal. Keep calcium and iron supplements away from it; about 4 hours is the usual advice, though the guideline calls that gap untested. Coffee, and in case reports soy and fiber, can also cut absorption, which is one more reason to take it well before breakfast. This is the one thyroid rule with clear evidence and it is a timing rule, not a food rule.
rules.separate_hours_note: calcium and iron supplements; the ATA 2014 guideline calls the 4-hour gap traditional but untested

rules.text: Iodine: adequate (150 mcg/day) but not excessive; excess iodine (kelp supplements) can worsen thyroid disease.
rules.why: Get enough iodine, about 150 mcg a day, but not extra. Kelp and iodine supplements can make thyroid disease worse.

rules.text: Goitrogens (cruciferous vegetables, soy): not a concern at normal intake with adequate iodine.
Gluten-free for Hashimoto's: no evidence unless celiac disease is present (which is more common in autoimmune thyroid disease, so screening is reasonable).
Hyperthyroidism: adequate calories and calcium during active disease; avoid iodine excess.

conflicts.text: Soy is fine at normal intake with adequate iodine; only the levothyroxine timing separation applies.
Keep iron supplements about 4 hours from levothyroxine (the usual advice; the ATA guideline calls the gap untested). The Plan shows the timing rule; the app does not move meals on the clock.

education.plain: There is no thyroid diet. The one rule with clear evidence is about timing your medication: take levothyroxine the same way every day, on an empty stomach 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime 3 or more hours after the evening meal, and keep calcium and iron supplements away from it (about 4 hours is the usual advice). Get enough iodine (150 mcg a day) but not extra; kelp supplements can make thyroid disease worse. Broccoli, cabbage, and soy are fine at normal amounts. Going gluten-free for Hashimoto's has no evidence unless you also have celiac disease, which is worth screening for.
evidence: ATA hypothyroidism guideline (2014): levothyroxine 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime, 3 or more hours after the evening meal (weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence); separate from calcium and iron supplements, a 4-hour gap being traditional but untested (weak recommendation, weak evidence). Coffee reduces absorption; case reports link soy and fiber.
Iodine adequate (150 mcg/day) but not excessive; excess iodine (kelp supplements) can worsen thyroid disease.
Goitrogens are not a concern at normal intake with adequate iodine.
contested: Selenium supplementation: mixed evidence.
Gluten-free for Hashimoto's: no evidence unless celiac disease is present; celiac disease is more common in autoimmune thyroid disease, so screening is reasonable.
do_not_claim: Do not recommend selenium supplementation.
Do not encode a "thyroid diet".
Do not encode gluten-free for Hashimoto's without celiac disease.
Do not restrict cruciferous vegetables or soy as goitrogens at normal intake.

modules.name: Pediatric nutrition (adults-only gate; caregiver mode for celiac and allergies)

evidence.summary: Rating: STRONG evidence base for pediatric celiac, food allergy, and type 1 diabetes; STRONG for the 2023 AAP obesity guideline; the problem is not evidence, it is safety and law.

tier2.label: Any pediatric nutrition number
tier2.consensus: None applied by the app. Growth, not weight loss, is the goal for almost every child.
tier2.why: Pediatric anything is Tier 2. Everything pediatric beyond caregiver-managed celiac disease and diagnosed food allergies (obesity, T1D, IBD, elimination diets) requires a pediatric clinician or is deferred.

age_gate.note: The app is for adults 18-plus. Hard age gate on the account holder.

caregiver_mode.note: A parent may manage a child's confirmed celiac disease or diagnosed food allergies, both of which have unambiguous, non-restrictive-beyond-necessity rules and a large practical need. Pediatrician-reviewed content per D10; the stage note substitutes the owner's review plus the citation trail.

rules.text: The app is for adults 18-plus. Full stop for v1's consumer posture.

Caregiver mode: a parent manages a child's confirmed celiac disease or diagnosed food allergies only. Everything else pediatric (obesity, T1D, IBD, elimination diets) requires a pediatric clinician or comes later.
Growth, not weight loss, is the goal for almost every child. The AAP 2023 guideline endorses intensive treatment for pediatric obesity, delivered by clinicians, not apps.

Restrictive diets in children (low FODMAP, low histamine, ketogenic, elimination diets) carry growth and disordered-eating risk that pediatric GI and allergy societies warn about repeatedly. Not offered.
Pediatric type 1 diabetes carbohydrate counting is insulin dosing by another name. That is medical and not offered.
Early allergen introduction (peanut at 4 to 6 months reduces allergy; LEAP and EAT trials; now AAP and AAAAI consensus) is background for caregivers, not an app feature.

COPPA: any user under 13 requires verifiable parental consent and strict data handling; Apple and Google impose additional rules on health apps aimed at minors. The account holder is always the adult.

education.plain: This app is for adults. The one thing a parent can do here is manage a child's confirmed celiac disease or diagnosed food allergies, because those rules are clear and do not restrict more than necessary. Children's weight, type 1 diabetes, IBD, and any elimination diet belong with a pediatric clinician; growth, not weight loss, is the goal for almost every child, and restrictive diets carry real growth and eating-disorder risk.
evidence: AAP 2023 obesity guideline endorses intensive treatment for pediatric obesity, delivered by clinicians, not apps.
NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN pediatric celiac guidelines and NIAID food allergy guidelines: unambiguous rules with a large practical need.
LEAP and EAT trials: peanut introduction at 4 to 6 months reduces allergy; now AAP and AAAAI consensus.
Pediatric T1D carbohydrate counting is insulin dosing by another name.
do_not_claim: Do not allow account holders under 18.
Do not offer any pediatric feature beyond caregiver-managed celiac disease and diagnosed food allergies.
Do not offer weight loss, T1D carbohydrate counting, IBD, or elimination diets for children.
Do not apply any pediatric nutrition number; all pediatric numbers are Tier 2.

modules.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
modules.phase1_ref: Added Sept 9, 2026 at the owner’s request; evidence reviewed against the 2022 ACR integrative-interventions guideline and 2021 EULAR lifestyle recommendations

evidence.summary: MODERATE for a Mediterranean-style eating pattern (ACR 2022: conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence); INSUFFICIENT for every other named diet (ACR conditionally recommends against formally defined diets and dietary supplements); medication is the treatment.

rules.text: Follow a Mediterranean-style eating pattern. The ACR guideline conditionally recommends it for people with RA; the certainty of evidence is low, and the benefit seen in trials is modest symptom improvement, not disease control.

No other formally defined diet (vegan, ketogenic, elimination, gluten-free without celiac disease, nightshade-free, paleo) is recommended for RA. The ACR guideline conditionally recommends against them because evidence is lacking and restriction has costs.
Dietary supplements, including fish oil, are not recommended by the ACR guideline for RA. Omega-3 from fish as food fits the Mediterranean pattern; supplement questions go to the rheumatologist.
If overweight, weight management is part of care: excess weight is associated with higher disease activity and worse response to treatment (EULAR 2021).
Alcohol: if you take methotrexate or leflunomide, ask your prescriber what limit applies to you. The app does not set an alcohol limit for RA.
Not a food rule, but the one lifestyle factor with the strongest RA evidence: stopping smoking improves disease activity and treatment response (EULAR 2021).

conflicts.text: Both point to a Mediterranean or DASH pattern.
Same pattern; selecting both adds nothing.

education.plain: There is no diet that treats rheumatoid arthritis. Disease-modifying medication does that. The one eating pattern with guideline support is Mediterranean-style, and even that is a conditional recommendation on low-certainty evidence: some trials show modest improvement in pain and stiffness. The named diets sold online for RA (elimination, nightshade-free, gluten-free without celiac disease) do not have evidence behind them and the ACR recommends against them.
evidence: ACR 2022: conditional recommendation for a Mediterranean-style diet; conditional recommendation against other formally defined diets and against dietary supplements.
EULAR 2021 lifestyle recommendations: healthy balanced diet, weight management if overweight, smoking cessation; no specific diet endorsed.
contested: Fish-oil supplements have trials showing small symptom benefits; the ACR still does not recommend supplements. Discuss with your rheumatologist.
Elimination diets produce reports of benefit in individuals; blinded evidence is lacking.
do_not_claim: Any diet treats, cures, or replaces medication for RA.
Nightshades, gluten, or dairy cause RA flares in general.
Supplements are recommended.

evidence.summary: MODERATE for dietary fiber (especially psyllium) and fluid; MODERATE for two green kiwifruit a day (one well-designed RCT); LIMITED for prunes; medication is the next step when diet is not enough.

rules.text: Fiber 25 to 38 g a day from whole plant foods, increased gradually over 2 to 3 weeks with extra fluid. Too fast causes gas and bloating.
rules.why: Fiber and fluid are the first step, and they work for many people.

rules.text: Drink enough that urine is pale. Fiber without fluid can make constipation worse.
Two green kiwifruit a day improved constipation and abdominal comfort in a multicenter RCT, with fewer side effects than psyllium.
Psyllium (a soluble fiber supplement) is the fiber with the best trial evidence for constipation. It is a supplement, so it is a conversation with your clinician or pharmacist, not an app rule.
Prefer whole fruit, vegetables, whole grains, beans, nuts and seeds.
Regular meals, especially breakfast, and daily physical activity support a regular bowel habit.
New constipation after age 50, blood in stool, weight loss, or constipation that does not respond to fiber needs a clinician visit, not more fiber.

conflicts.text: Gastroparesis texture rules win; meet fiber through soft, cooked, and blended sources.
Many high-fiber foods are high FODMAP; the elimination phase is time-limited.
In an IBD flare the low-residue rules win.

education.plain: Fiber and fluid are the first step for constipation, and they work for many people. Increase fiber slowly. Two green kiwifruit a day is a food option with real trial evidence. If diet does not fix it within a few weeks, that is what medication is for; do not keep piling on fiber.
evidence: AGA-ACG 2023 guideline: fiber supplementation (psyllium) is a reasonable first step; several over-the-counter and prescription options follow.
Kiwifruit RCT 2023: two green kiwifruit daily improved complete spontaneous bowel movements versus psyllium and prunes.
contested: Prunes have small trials with benefit; the evidence base is thinner than kiwifruit or psyllium.
Wheat bran helps some and worsens bloating in others.
do_not_claim: Detox teas, cleanses, or colon cleanses treat constipation.
Coffee is a treatment (it stimulates some people; it is not a therapy).

evidence.summary: STRONG for weight loss in people with overweight and knee or hip OA (ACR/AF 2019 strong recommendation; IDEA RCT: 10 percent loss improved pain and function); LIMITED for any specific diet composition; supplements are conditionally recommended against.

rules.text: If overweight: weight loss is the strongest diet-related lever for knee and hip OA. In the IDEA trial, losing 10 percent of body weight cut pain and improved function; 5 percent helped less.
A Mediterranean-style pattern is a reasonable default. Evidence that diet composition itself changes OA symptoms is limited.
Exercise is a core treatment for OA, with weight loss when relevant. The diet supports it; it does not replace it.
Glucosamine, chondroitin, fish oil, vitamin D and other supplements are conditionally recommended against for OA by the ACR/AF guideline. Not encoded as rules.

conflicts.text: Same weight goal; the weight module carries the detail.

education.plain: For knee and hip osteoarthritis, the diet lever that works is weight loss, if you carry extra weight. Ten percent of body weight is the target the strongest trial used. Beyond weight, no specific eating pattern has good evidence for OA symptoms, and the guideline recommends against most supplements marketed for joints.
evidence: ACR/AF 2019: strong recommendation for weight loss in overweight patients with knee or hip OA.
IDEA trial: diet plus exercise producing about 10 percent weight loss reduced knee pain and inflammatory markers over 18 months.
contested: Turmeric and curcumin have small trials with short follow-up; not a recommendation.
Anti-inflammatory diet claims for OA are extrapolated, not tested.
do_not_claim: Any food or supplement rebuilds cartilage.
Glucosamine or chondroitin are recommended.

evidence.summary: STRONG for carbohydrate counting matched to insulin (DAFNE RCT; ADA Standards of Care); insulin ratios and correction factors are clinician-set and the app never doses insulin.

tier2.label: Insulin dosing
tier2.consensus: The app never calculates or suggests insulin doses. Carbohydrate-to-insulin ratios and correction factors come from the diabetes team.

rules.text: Count carbohydrate at each meal and match insulin using the ratio your diabetes team set. The app shows carbohydrate grams per recipe and food; it never suggests an insulin dose.
Low blood sugar: 15 g of fast carbohydrate (glucose tablets, 4 oz juice), recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a snack if the next meal is more than an hour away (ADA).
The same healthy eating patterns as type 2 diabetes apply: Mediterranean, DASH, or plant-forward, with carbohydrate quality and fiber.
Sugar-sweetened beverages outside of treating a low.
Alcohol can cause delayed low blood sugar, especially overnight. Eat with it and check glucose.
Celiac disease is more common with type 1 diabetes. Screening is standard; if you have symptoms or it was never checked, ask.
Very low carbohydrate or ketogenic eating with insulin needs your diabetes team involved first because of hypoglycemia and ketoacidosis risk.

conflicts.text: Insulin-treated diabetes plus very low carbohydrate needs clinician sign-off first (hypoglycemia, ketoacidosis).
Same eating-pattern rules.
Common together; rules do not conflict.

medication_questions.text: Do you take an SGLT2 inhibitor (for example empagliflozin, dapagliflozin)?

education.plain: With type 1 diabetes, food and insulin are matched meal by meal. Carbohydrate counting is the skill that makes that work, and it has strong trial evidence for better control and more freedom in what you eat. This app shows carbohydrate grams for every food and recipe. It never tells you how much insulin to take; that number comes from your diabetes team.
evidence: DAFNE RCT: structured carbohydrate counting and dose adjustment improved HbA1c and quality of life.
ADA Standards of Care: individualized MNT, carbohydrate counting for people on multiple daily injections or pumps.
contested: Low-carbohydrate approaches in T1D have supporters and small studies; the safety issues are real and clinician involvement is required.
do_not_claim: The app can dose insulin or replace diabetes education.

evidence.summary: MODERATE for a high-fiber pattern after recovery from diverticulitis (AGA conditional recommendation); STRONG that nuts, seeds, corn and popcorn do not need to be avoided (large cohort, guideline-endorsed); temporary low-fiber or liquid diet during an acute episode is clinician-directed.

rules.text: After recovery, a high-fiber, high-quality diet (vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes) is advised.
Nuts, seeds, corn and popcorn do not need to be avoided. The old advice was overturned by a large prospective study, and the AGA recommends against restricting them.
Higher red and processed meat intake is associated with more diverticulitis in cohort data; a plant-forward pattern is reasonable.
During an acute episode, follow your clinician’s instructions (often clear liquids then low-fiber for a few days), and return to high fiber as symptoms settle.

conflicts.text: Both favor fiber.
Both favor fiber and plant diversity.

education.plain: Between episodes, eat more fiber, not less. Nuts, seeds, and popcorn are fine; that restriction was disproven. During an acute diverticulitis episode, follow your clinician’s short-term instructions, then go back to the high-fiber pattern.
evidence: AGA 2015 guideline: high-fiber diet after acute diverticulitis (conditional, very low quality evidence); advises against avoiding nuts and popcorn.
Strate 2008 (Health Professionals Follow-up Study): nut and popcorn intake was associated with lower, not higher, diverticulitis risk.
contested: Whether fiber prevents recurrence is uncertain; the recommendation rests on low-quality evidence and overall health benefit.
do_not_claim: Seeds or nuts get stuck in diverticula and cause attacks.

modules.name: DASH eating pattern
modules.phase1_ref: Added Sept 9, 2026 (pattern entry for the DASH rules already used by hypertension)

evidence.summary: STRONG: DASH lowered blood pressure in randomized feeding trials and is a Class 1, Level A recommendation in the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline; also endorsed for diabetes and heart health.

rules.text: Vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, beans, nuts.
Limit red meat, sweets, sugar-sweetened beverages, and full-fat dairy.
Sodium under 2,300 mg a day; 1,500 mg lowered blood pressure further in DASH-Sodium.
rules.why: Cutting to 1,500 mg lowered blood pressure further in the DASH-Sodium trial.

rules.text: Saturated fat under 10 percent of calories.
rules.why: Keep saturated fat under 10 percent of calories.

conflicts.text: Hypertension already applies DASH.
DASH is potassium-rich; CKD potassium limits win.

education.plain: DASH is the eating pattern with the best blood-pressure evidence there is: it was tested in controlled feeding trials, not just surveys. It is also a good general pattern for heart health and diabetes.
evidence: DASH trial 1997: the pattern lowered systolic blood pressure by about 5.5 mmHg overall and 11 mmHg in people with hypertension.
DASH-Sodium 2001: cutting sodium to 1,500 mg lowered pressure further.
contested: Population sodium targets are debated; for people with hypertension the guideline position is clear.
do_not_claim: DASH replaces blood-pressure medication.

evidence.summary: MODERATE: a randomized trial of the four cholesterol-lowering food groups lowered LDL about 13 percent under real-world advice; referenced in AHA 2021 dietary guidance.

rules.text: Build meals around the four Portfolio groups: viscous fiber (oats, barley, psyllium, okra, eggplant), soy and other legume protein, nuts (about a handful a day), and plant sterol-enriched foods.
Low saturated fat, as in the trial.
rules.why: Keep saturated fat low, under 7 percent of calories as in the trial, and limit processed meat, full-fat dairy, and fried food.

rules.text: Plant sterols (2 g a day) come mainly from fortified spreads and supplements; that is a choice to make with the evidence in view, not an app rule.
Limit processed meat, full-fat dairy, and fried foods.

conflicts.text: Portfolio is a stronger version of the heart-healthy rules.
Soy protein is one of the four Portfolio groups; without soy, use other legumes and nuts.
Legumes and some nuts are high FODMAP; elimination is time-limited.

education.plain: The Portfolio diet stacks four food groups that each lower LDL cholesterol a little: sticky (viscous) fiber, soy and bean protein, nuts, and plant sterols. Together, in a randomized trial, they lowered LDL by about 13 percent with ordinary dietary advice. It is a food-first option for people who want to push LDL down before or alongside medication.
evidence: Jenkins 2011 JAMA: 13.8 percent LDL reduction with intensive advice, 13.1 percent with routine advice, over 6 months.
contested: Plant sterols are borderline supplement territory; food-based sources are limited.
do_not_claim: The Portfolio diet replaces statins when a clinician recommends them.

evidence.summary: MODERATE for weight loss, and no better than ordinary calorie restriction (NEJM 2022 RCT); earlier eating windows may help cardiometabolic markers (JAMA Intern Med 2022); LIMITED long-term data; not for pregnancy, insulin users without clinician input, or history of disordered eating.

rules.text: Eat within an 8 to 10 hour window (for example 8 am to 6 pm) and take only water, plain tea, or black coffee outside it. Earlier windows had better markers in trials than late ones.

In the largest trial, adding a time window to calorie restriction did not produce more weight loss than calorie restriction alone. The window helps some people eat less; it is not a mechanism on its own.
What you eat inside the window still follows your other rules.
Not appropriate in pregnancy or breastfeeding, and needs clinician input if you use insulin or a sulfonylurea (hypoglycemia). Skip it if you have a history of disordered eating.

conflicts.text: Fasting windows with insulin need the diabetes team involved.
Fine for most people with type 2 diabetes not on insulin or sulfonylureas; otherwise ask.
Small frequent meals win over a compressed window.

medication_questions.text: Do you use insulin or a sulfonylurea (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride)?

education.plain: Time-restricted eating means eating inside a set window each day. It can help people eat less, and the weight loss in trials is real but no larger than plain calorie restriction. If it makes eating simpler for you, it is a reasonable tool. It is not for pregnancy, and insulin users need their team involved.
evidence: Liu 2022 NEJM: 12 months of calorie restriction with or without an 8-hour window produced the same weight loss.
Jamshed 2022 JAMA Intern Med: an early 8-hour window improved weight and some cardiometabolic markers versus a 12-hour-plus window over 14 weeks.
contested: Late-night eating windows appear less helpful than early ones; evidence is short-term.
do_not_claim: Fasting windows have unique metabolic effects beyond eating less.

modules.name: Medicines that interact with food
modules.phase1_ref: Added 2026-09-10 after the dietitian review; not covered in the Phase 1 document

evidence.summary: Rating: MODERATE for keeping vitamin K steady on warfarin (systematic review: cutting dietary vitamin K does not improve anticoagulation; steady habits are the advice that follows); STRONG for grapefruit, Seville orange, lime, and pomelo with medicines cleared by CYP3A4 (pharmacokinetic evidence); MODERATE for levothyroxine timing (ATA guideline: weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence; the calcium and iron gap is a weak recommendation on weak evidence).

medication_questions.text: Has a pharmacist or doctor told you to avoid grapefruit with one of your medicines? (Common with simvastatin, lovastatin, atorvastatin, some blood pressure and heart rhythm medicines, and some transplant medicines.)

rules.text: Warfarin: keep vitamin K steady rather than low. Eat about the same amount of leafy greens and other vitamin K foods from week to week, and tell the clinic that manages your INR before a big change in diet, a new supplement, or regular cranberry or grapefruit juice. Do not cut greens out; a sudden drop swings the INR as much as a sudden rise.

Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, Seville orange (often in marmalade), pomelo, and lime while on the medicine your pharmacist flagged. They block the gut enzyme that clears the drug, so blood levels rise, and the effect lasts about a day, so taking them hours apart does not fix it. Sweet oranges, such as navel or Valencia, are fine.

Levothyroxine: take it the same way every day, with water on an empty stomach, either 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime, 3 or more hours after the evening meal. Keep calcium and iron supplements away from it; about 4 hours is the usual advice, though the guideline calls that gap untested. Coffee, and in case reports soy and fiber, can also cut absorption, which is one more reason to take it well before breakfast.
rules.separate_hours_note: calcium and iron supplements; the ATA 2014 guideline calls the 4-hour gap traditional but untested

education.plain: A few common medicines react with food. If you take warfarin, keep the amount of leafy greens and other vitamin K foods about the same from week to week rather than cutting them out, and tell the clinic that checks your INR before a big change in how you eat. If a pharmacist or doctor has told you to avoid grapefruit with one of your medicines, that includes grapefruit juice, Seville oranges, pomelos, and limes, and spacing them hours apart does not fix it; sweet oranges are fine. If you take levothyroxine, take it the same way every day with water, either 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime, and keep calcium and iron supplements away from it. Your doctor or pharmacist knows your medicines; ask them before you change anything.
evidence: Warfarin: restricting dietary vitamin K does not improve anticoagulation; keeping intake steady is the advice that follows (Violi 2016, systematic review).

Grapefruit, Seville orange, lime, and pomelo carry furanocoumarins that switch off gut CYP3A4 until new enzyme is made, so the effect lasts about a day; sweet oranges such as navel and Valencia do not (Bailey 2013).
Levothyroxine: 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime, 3 or more hours after the evening meal; separate from calcium and iron supplements, a 4-hour gap being traditional but untested (ATA 2014).
do_not_claim: Do not tell anyone on warfarin to avoid leafy greens.
Do not claim that all citrus interacts with medicines.
Do not suggest a dose, or a time that differs from what the prescriber set.
